title: Postings lists
description: An inverted index maps every term to a postings list — the sorted document ids containing that term, plus positions for phrase queries. The list is the unit of retrieval: a query for two terms intersects their lists. Everything else in this database (compression, skip lists, bitmaps) exists to make these lists smaller and their intersection faster.
mechanism: During indexing, append each (term, doc_id) pair to the term's list; at segment flush, sort each list by doc id. Query: walk the two sorted lists with two pointers, emitting ids present in both.
algo: Two-pointer intersection of lists of length m and n is O(m + n). Sorted order is what makes merge-based retrieval possible at all.

title: Gap (d-gap) encoding
description: Document ids in a postings list are sorted, so instead of storing each full id we store the gap to the previous one — small numbers dominate, and small numbers compress well. A list like [1000, 1005, 1007, 1040] becomes [1000, 5, 2, 33]. Gap encoding is the first transform applied by virtually every postings codec before the bits are packed.
mechanism: Encode: gaps[0] = ids[0], gaps[i] = ids[i] - ids[i-1]. Decode: running prefix sum. Gaps are then fed to a variable-byte or bit-packing codec.
algo: Encoding and decoding are O(n) with tiny constants. Average gap for n docs over D doc ids is D/n, so dense terms get tiny gaps.
demo:
ids = [1000, 1005, 1007, 1040, 1041, 1100]

def to_gaps(xs):
    return [xs[0]] + [b - a for a, b in zip(xs, xs[1:])]

def from_gaps(gs):
    out, run = [], 0
    for g in gs:
        run += g
        out.append(run)
    return out

gaps = to_gaps(ids)
print('ids :', ids)
print('gaps:', gaps)
print('round-trip ok:', from_gaps(gaps) == ids)
print('max value to store drops %d -> %d' % (max(ids), max(gaps)))

title: Variable-byte (vByte) codes
description: Variable-byte encoding stores each integer in 7-bit chunks with a continuation bit, so small gaps take one byte and large ones take more. It decodes fast with simple loops and needs no tables, which is why it survived decades of fancier codecs. The trade is density: it uses whole bytes where bit-level codecs would use fewer bits.
mechanism: Write the integer 7 bits at a time, low chunk first, setting the high bit on the final chunk. Decode: accumulate chunks until a byte with the high bit set appears.
algo: O(bytes) per integer, branch-light. Values under 128 cost 1 byte; each extra 7 bits costs another byte.

title: Elias-Fano encoding
description: Elias-Fano stores a sorted integer sequence in close to the information-theoretic minimum space while still supporting random access. It splits each value into high and low bits: low bits in a flat array, high bits as a unary-coded bitvector with select support. Monotone postings lists compress to about 2 bits per element over the optimum.
mechanism: For n values under universe u: low = log2(u/n) bits stored directly; high bits stored as gaps in unary (value i sets bit i + gap). Select on the bitvector recovers any element without decoding the whole list.
algo: Access is O(1) with select structures. Space is n*ceil(log2(u/n)) + 2n bits — near optimal for monotone sequences.
demo:
# Elias-Fano, simplified: split values into high/low bits.
vals = [3, 7, 8, 15, 16, 23, 24, 31]
n, u = len(vals), 32
import math
low_bits = max(1, math.ceil(math.log2(u / n)))
low_mask = (1 << low_bits) - 1
lows = [v & low_mask for v in vals]
highs = [v >> low_bits for v in vals]
print('values :', vals)
print('low bits (%d each):' % low_bits, lows)
print('high parts:', highs, '(stored as unary gaps in the real codec)')
# random access: recombine without scanning
print('element 5 =', (highs[5] << low_bits) | lows[5], '(O(1) select in real EF)')

title: Roaring bitmaps
description: Roaring bitmaps store sets of 32-bit integers as 65,536 containers keyed by the high 16 bits: sparse containers are sorted arrays, dense ones are 8KB bitmaps, and long runs become run-length containers. Set operations (AND/OR/XOR) run container-by-container, often using SIMD. They routinely beat both hash sets and plain bitmaps for postings-like workloads.
mechanism: Split each int into high16 (container key) and low16 (member). Choose the container type by cardinality: array under 4096, bitmap above, run container for consecutive runs. Operations align containers by key and combine pairwise.
algo: AND of two bitmaps is O(number of set words) with SIMD; array containers intersect in O(m+n). Space adapts to density automatically.

title: Term dictionaries and FSTs
description: The term dictionary maps each distinct term to its postings pointer, and with millions of terms it must be tiny and fast. Finite-state transducers (FSTs) compile the sorted term set into a minimal automaton that stores shared prefixes once — Lucene's terms index fits millions of terms in tens of megabytes. Lookup walks the automaton byte by byte: O(term length), no hash table needed.
mechanism: Build a minimal deterministic acyclic FST over (term bytes -> postings offset). Shared prefixes share states; the output value accumulates along the path. Block-based terms dicts on disk pair with an in-memory FST index over block prefixes.
algo: Lookup is O(term length) transitions. Construction is O(total term bytes) via sorted-input minimization.

title: Skip lists in postings
description: Intersecting a long postings list with a short one by linear scan wastes time on the long list. Skip lists store jump pointers every B entries so the merge can skip ahead to the region that matters. Lucene stores skip data per block; galloping (exponential) search gives a similar effect without explicit pointers. Either way, the long list is traversed in jumps, not steps.
mechanism: Every B-th entry records (doc_id, file_offset). To advance past target doc d, binary- or linear-search the skip table for the last entry <= d, then seek and scan linearly within one block.
algo: Advancing past d costs O(number of skips) then O(B) linear scan. Intersection of m,n lists improves toward O(m log(n/m)) with galloping.
demo:
docs = list(range(0, 10000, 3))          # long postings list
B = 64
skips = [(docs[i], i) for i in range(0, len(docs), B)]  # (doc_id, index)

def advance(target):
    steps = 0
    idx = 0
    for doc_id, pos in skips:          # jump over whole blocks
        steps += 1
        if doc_id <= target:
            idx = pos
        else:
            break
    while docs[idx] < target:          # linear scan inside one block
        idx += 1
        steps += 1
    return docs[idx], steps

doc, steps = advance(7777)
print('found doc', doc, 'in', steps, 'steps (vs', len(docs), 'linear)')

title: Block-based postings (FOR/PForDelta)
description: Frame-of-reference and Patched Frame-of-Reference codecs process postings in blocks of 128 integers: find the block's bit width, pack all values at that width, and patch the few outliers separately. PForDelta decodes over 2 billion integers per second on modern CPUs because the inner loop is branch-free SIMD. It is the workhorse codec behind Lucene's Lucene90 postings.
mechanism: Per 128-int block: compute max bits b needed (minus outliers), bit-pack at width b, store outlier values and positions as patches. Decode: unpack b-bit values, then apply patches.
algo: O(block size) per block with tiny constants; SIMD unpack processes 4-8 ints per instruction. Outlier patching keeps the common width small.
demo:
# Frame-of-reference: store offsets from the block minimum at fixed width.
block = [1000, 1002, 1001, 1005, 1003, 1007, 1002, 1004]
base = min(block)
offsets = [v - base for v in block]
width = max(o.bit_length() for o in offsets)
print('block :', block)
print('base=%d, max offset=%d -> %d bits per value' % (base, max(offsets), width))
print('packed bits: %d vs %d unpacked (32-bit)' % (len(block) * width, len(block) * 32))
decoded = [base + o for o in offsets]
print('round-trip ok:', decoded == block)

title: Positions and offsets
description: Phrase and proximity queries need more than document ids — they need term positions within each document. Positions are stored as a second compressed list per (term, doc) pair, gap-encoded like doc ids. Offsets (character start/end) add one more layer for highlighting. They multiply index size, so engines store them only for indexed fields that need phrase search.
mechanism: Per term per doc: store sorted positions, gap-encoded; per position optionally store (start_offset, end_offset) as two more gap lists. Phrase 'a b' matches when a position of b equals a position of a plus 1.
algo: Phrase check is O(pos_a + pos_b) merge per doc. Storage is roughly proportional to total term occurrences, not documents.
complexity: O(pos_a + pos_b) per doc phrase check
demo:
pos = {'quick': [2, 9], 'brown': [3, 10], 'fox': [4]}  # term -> positions in doc 7

def phrase(a, b):  # does 'a b' occur consecutively?
    pa, pb = pos[a], pos[b]
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(pa) and j < len(pb):
        if pb[j] == pa[i] + 1:
            return True
        if pb[j] < pa[i] + 1:
            j += 1
        else:
            i += 1
    return False

print('"quick brown" phrase:', phrase('quick', 'brown'))
print('"brown quick" phrase:', phrase('brown', 'quick'))

title: Doc values (columnar)
description: Inverted indexes answer 'which docs contain term X'; doc values answer 'what is field Y of doc D' — the columnar flip used for sorting, faceting, and aggregations. Stored doc-id-major instead of term-major, they stream sequentially during aggregations instead of random-accessing postings. Modern engines keep both: inverted for search, doc values for analytics.
mechanism: At index time, write per-field per-doc values into a columnar store (one column per field), compressed by type ( numerics with FOR, strings with dictionary encoding). At query time, iterate the matched doc set and look up columns by doc id.
algo: Lookup is O(1) per doc per field. Aggregation over m matches is O(m) sequential reads — cache-friendly.

print('avg price of matches: %.2f (columnar lookup, no postings walk)' % avg)

title: Ranked retrieval on compressed lists
description: Compression must not break scoring: BM25 needs term frequency and document length while intersecting compressed postings. Engines decode blocks lazily and compute partial scores per block, using WAND-style upper bounds to skip blocks that cannot enter the top-k. The result is ranked retrieval at nearly the speed of uncompressed indexes, at a fraction of the memory.
mechanism: Store per-doc term frequency alongside doc ids (compressed with the same codecs). Maintain each term's max score contribution; during top-k traversal, skip any block whose upper bound cannot beat the current k-th best score.
algo: WAND reduces scoring work toward O(k log n) in practice. Block-max bounds prune whole blocks without decoding them.
complexity: near O(k log n) with pruning vs O(n) naive
demo:
# WAND idea: skip blocks whose max possible score can't beat current threshold.
blocks = [  # (block_max_score, doc_scores)
    (0.9, [(1, 0.8), (2, 0.9)]),
    (0.2, [(3, 0.1), (4, 0.2)]),
    (0.7, [(5, 0.6), (6, 0.7)]),
]
threshold = 0.5  # current k-th best score
scored, skipped = [], 0
for bmax, docs in blocks:
    if bmax < threshold:
        skipped += 1       # whole block pruned: no decode, no scoring
        continue
    scored.extend(docs)
print('scored docs:', scored)
print('blocks pruned without decoding:', skipped, 'of', len(blocks))

title: Index size vs speed tradeoffs
description: Every postings codec sits on a size-speed curve: Elias-Fano is tiny but slower to decode, PForDelta is fast but larger, uncompressed is fastest and huge. The right choice depends on the bottleneck — memory-bound systems pick smaller, CPU-bound systems pick faster. Most engines compromise: PForDelta-like codecs that decode at gigabytes per second while using a few bits per posting.
mechanism: Benchmark candidate codecs on your own postings distribution (gaps vary wildly by term frequency). Measure bits-per-posting and decode millions/sec; pick the knee of the curve, possibly per-field (positions get a denser codec than doc ids).
algo: Decision is empirical: measure both axes on representative data. No codec dominates on both axes simultaneously (information theory + CPU reality).
demo:
import math
# toy model: bits/posting vs decode speed for codec families
codecs = {
    'uncompressed-32bit': (32.0, 4000),
    'vbyte': (9.5, 900),
    'pfor-delta': (6.2, 2200),
    'elias-fano': (4.1, 350),
}
print('%-18s %10s %14s' % ('codec', 'bits/post', 'Mints/sec'))
for name, (bits, speed) in codecs.items():
    print('%-18s %10.1f %14d' % (name, bits, speed))
print('-> pfor-delta sits at the knee: small AND fast (why Lucene uses it)')

title: Building postings at scale
description: Nobody sorts a billion postings in RAM: large indexes are built with external merge — index documents in memory-sized chunks, flush sorted runs to disk, then k-way merge the runs into the final postings. Each flush is independently compressed, and the merge streams through them without decompressing everything at once. This is how a laptop-scale program builds a web-scale index.
mechanism: In-memory buffer of (term, doc) pairs; when full, sort by (term, doc) and flush a compressed run. Merge R runs with a heap over (term, doc) cursors, writing final postings term by term.
algo: External sort is O(n log n) total with O(buffer) memory. The k-way merge is O(n log R) for R runs.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(buffer) memory
demo:
import heapq

# simulate: 3 flushed runs, each sorted (term, doc); k-way merge them
runs = [
    [('a', 1), ('b', 2), ('c', 5)],
    [('a', 3), ('b', 4)],
    [('a', 2), ('c', 1)],
]
cursors = [iter(r) for r in runs]
heap = []
for i, cur in enumerate(cursors):
    try:
        heap.append((next(cur), i))
    except StopIteration:
        pass
heapq.heapify(heap)
merged = []
while heap:
    (term, doc), i = heapq.heappop(heap)
    merged.append((term, doc))
    try:
        heapq.heappush(heap, (next(cursors[i]), i))
    except StopIteration:
        pass
print('merged postings:', merged)

title: Query-time decompression budgets
description: Decompression is only free if it stays off the critical path: engines budget microseconds per query for codec work and pick algorithms that fit. Block codecs decode 128 integers in a few hundred nanoseconds with SIMD; the query planner prefetches the next block while scoring the current one. When p99 latency spikes, the codec is rarely the cause — but the block size and prefetch distance are the first knobs to check.
mechanism: Decode one block at a time into a small reusable buffer; overlap the next block's fetch with current-block scoring. Keep blocks small enough to stay in L1/L2 cache during the merge.
algo: Amortized decode cost is O(1) per posting with SIMD; prefetch hides memory latency so the merge loop rarely stalls.
demo:
import time

# measure gap-decode throughput: the query-time budget reality check
ids = list(range(0, 1000000, 7))
gaps = [ids[0]] + [b - a for a, b in zip(ids, ids[1:])]

t = time.perf_counter()
run, out = 0, []
for g in gaps:
    run += g
    out.append(run)
dt = time.perf_counter() - t
print('decoded %d postings in %.3f s -> %.0f M postings/sec' % (len(gaps), dt, len(gaps) / dt / 1e6))
print('a 10k-posting query spends ~%.1f us decoding' % (10000 / (len(gaps) / dt) * 1e6))

title: Compressed indices for vector payloads
description: Vector search borrows postings compression for its metadata: quantized vectors (product quantization codes) are stored per IVF list exactly like postings, and scalar filters use Roaring bitmaps to intersect with vector candidates. The same codecs — FOR, Roaring, vByte — compress both the text and vector sides of a hybrid index, which is why modern vector databases embed an inverted index rather than reinventing one.
mechanism: PQ codes per vector stored list-major (one byte array per IVF list); filter bitmaps per attribute value; query = bitmap AND over filters, then distance scan over the surviving PQ codes with asymmetric distance computation.
algo: PQ scan is O(d_sub * K) table lookups per vector; bitmap pre-filter reduces the candidate set before any distance math.
demo:
# PQ codes stored like postings: one byte array per IVF list; filter via bitmap.
import random
random.seed(8)
# 8 sub-quantizers, 256 centroids each -> 8 bytes per vector
pq_codes = [[random.randrange(256) for _ in range(8)] for _ in range(1000)]
# scalar filter: 'lang == en' as a bitmap (set of doc ids)
en_bitmap = set(i for i in range(1000) if i % 3 == 0)
# asymmetric distance: precomputed per-subquantizer tables vs query
tables = [[random.random() for _ in range(256)] for _ in range(8)]

def adc(code):
    return sum(tables[j][c] for j, c in enumerate(code))

cands = [i for i in en_bitmap]
best = min(cands, key=lambda i: adc(pq_codes[i]))
print('vectors: 1000, after filter: %d candidates' % len(cands))
print('best candidate id=%d approx-distance=%.3f (8 table lookups, no float vectors)' % (best, adc(pq_codes[best])))
